To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
movements in ROE for utilities are characterized by partial adjustment, and that the adjustment speed is sensitive to incentive rate regulation and the level of ROEs.

the time-series behavior for ROE for electric utilities follows the partial adjustment rather than a pure adjustment process implied under rate-of-return regulation, that the speed of adjustment for the ROE for electric utility is much longer than the corresponding speed of adjustment for manufacturing firms, and that the speed of the adjustment is sensitive to the level of the ROE and to the presence of incentive regulation.

the ROEs of utilities and manufacturing firms are partially adjusted, that the adjustment horizon is shorter for manufacturing firms, that the adjustment is more sensitive to incentive regulation, and that the adjustment is also more sensitive to the level of the ROE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behavior of ROEs for electric utilities and the implications for rate of return regulation.
the time-series behavior (i.e. the dynamics) of ROE for regulated firms.
the speed of adjustment in ROE for utilities and the implications of this behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rate-of-return regulation is not a pure cost-plus system.
rate regulation does not affect the speed of adjustment of the ROE for electric utilities.
rate of return regulation is not a perfect substitute for the competitive market, and the rate of adjustment of ROE is a key indicator of the efficiency of regulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate of change in ROE for utilities is not as fast as the change in rate base and the change in ROE is not as fast in the regulated industry as in nonregulated industries.

the ROE for electric utilities follows the behavior of a partial adjustment process, which is consistent with a cost-plus policy of regulation, and that incentive regulation can affect the speed of adjustment.
rate of return regulation has a significant effect on the behavior of the ROE of electric utilities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ROE of regulated firms is not a constant, but is subject to change over time.
ROEs for utilities adjust to their target levels at a slower speed than ROEs in manufacturing firms.
the ROE for electric utilities is not a random walk, but rather a slow-moving process that adjusts toward a target.
